subChunks.title: Concurrent Features: useTransition and useDeferredValue
subChunks.hookHtml: React 18 introduced concurrent rendering — the ability to interrupt, pause, and prioritise renders. Two hooks expose this capability to application code: useTransition for marking updates as non-urgent, and useDeferredValue for deferring derived state. These hooks let you keep the UI responsive during expensive renders without artificial debouncing.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The problem: blocking renders

A text input that filters a list of 10,000 items blocks the UI on every keystroke — the render is synchronous and can't be interrupted. The old fix was debounce (delay the update artificially). React 18's fix is to mark the update as lower priority so React can interrupt it if something more urgent arrives.

useTransition — marking updates as non-urgent

import { useState, useTransition } from 'react';

function SearchableQuestList({ quests }) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  const [filteredQuests, setFilteredQuests] = useState(quests);
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();

  function handleChange(e) {
    const value = e.target.value;
    setQuery(value); // Urgent — update the input immediately

    startTransition(() => {
      // Non-urgent — React can interrupt this if needed:
      setFilteredQuests(quests.filter(q => q.title.toLowerCase().includes(value)));
    });
  }

  return (
    <div>
      <input value={query} onChange={handleChange} placeholder="Search..." />
      {isPending && <span>Filtering...</span>}
      <ul>
        {filteredQuests.map(q => <li key={q.id}>{q.title}</li>)}
      </ul>
    </div>
  );
}

isPending is true while the transition is processing — use it to show a loading indicator without blocking the input.

useDeferredValue — deferring a value

useDeferredValue is the derived-value alternative to useTransition. It keeps the previous value until the new render is ready:

import { useState, useDeferredValue, useMemo } from 'react';

function SearchResults({ quests }) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query);

  // This expensive filter uses the deferred (possibly stale) value:
  const filtered = useMemo(
    () => quests.filter(q => q.title.toLowerCase().includes(deferredQuery)),
    [quests, deferredQuery]
  );

  const isStale = query !== deferredQuery;

  return (
    <div>
      <input value={query} onChange={e => setQuery(e.target.value)} />
      <ul style={{ opacity: isStale ? 0.5 : 1 }}>
        {filtered.map(q => <li key={q.id}>{q.title}</li>)}
      </ul>
    </div>
  );
}

useTransition vs useDeferredValue

// useTransition — you control which state update is deferred:
startTransition(() => setExpensiveState(value));

// useDeferredValue — you defer a derived value you don't own the setter for:
const deferred = useDeferredValue(propValue);

Vex: "These hooks require concurrent mode — React 18 with createRoot. They do not help with async operations like network requests — those are already non-blocking. They help with expensive synchronous renders: filtering huge lists, building complex derived data, or re-rendering large trees. Profile first; use these only when you've confirmed a render is blocking the UI."

When to use each

  • useTransition: when you control the state setter and want to mark a specific update as non-urgent. Best for: filtering, sorting, tab switching.
  • useDeferredValue: when you receive a value as a prop and can't control when it changes. Best for: expensive derived state in child components.

storyBeats.text: A search input that lags behind every keystroke. 10,000 quests filtered synchronously. The UI freezes for 200ms per character. Vex opens the React 18 docs.

storyBeats.text: Before React 18: debounce the input, delay the filter, accept the artificial lag. With React 18 concurrent mode: mark the filter update as a transition. React keeps the input responsive and interrupts the expensive render if another keystroke arrives. No artificial delay.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a filterable list that uses useTransition to keep the input responsive:

  • Generate 5000 mock quest items
  • Wire a search input to query state (urgent update)
  • Wrap the filter operation in startTransition
  • Show a 'Filtering...' label when isPending is true
  • Use data-testid="search" on the input and data-testid="pending" on the pending indicator
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a side-by-side comparison of debounced filtering (200ms delay with setTimeout) vs useTransition filtering for a list of 20,000 items. Show both implementations in the same component with a toggle. Add a frame rate counter using requestAnimationFrame that shows the current FPS. Write a comment explaining when each approach is appropriate.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what problem useTransition and useDeferredValue solve that debouncing doesn't solve cleanly. Walk through the difference between the two hooks — when would you use each? Then explain the isPending flag and what a good UX looks like while a transition is in progress.

questions.prompt: What does wrapping a state update in `startTransition` do?
options: Marks the update as non-urgent — React will process it after more urgent updates (like input changes) and can interrupt it if needed
Defers the update until the next animation frame
Batches the update with other state changes in the same event handler
Runs the update in a Web Worker to avoid blocking the main thread
questions.answer: Marks the update as non-urgent — React will process it after more urgent updates (like input changes) and can interrupt it if needed
questions.explanation: startTransition tells React that the enclosed state update is lower priority. If a higher-priority update arrives (like another keystroke), React can pause the transition render, handle the urgent update, then resume the transition. This keeps the UI responsive without artificial debouncing delays.

options: The transition is still rendering — a lower-priority update is in progress
A network request is in flight
The component is waiting for a useEffect to complete
questions.answer: The transition is still rendering — a lower-priority update is in progress
questions.explanation: isPending is true from when startTransition is called until the non-urgent render commits to the screen. Use it to show a loading indicator (a spinner, dimmed list, 'Filtering...' text) so the user knows work is in progress. The input remains fully interactive while isPending is true.

questions.prompt: When should you use `useDeferredValue` instead of `useTransition`?
options: When you receive a value as a prop or from context and can't control the state setter — useDeferredValue defers a value you don't own
When the deferred update involves a network request
When you need to cancel the transition programmatically
useDeferredValue is always preferable — it's the newer API
questions.answer: When you receive a value as a prop or from context and can't control the state setter — useDeferredValue defers a value you don't own
questions.explanation: useTransition requires access to the state setter — you call startTransition(() => setState(value)). If you receive a value as a prop (from a parent's state you don't control), you can't use useTransition. useDeferredValue(propValue) gives you a deferred version of that value — the component renders with the previous value until the new render is ready.

questions.prompt: Would useTransition help with a slow API response (a fetch that takes 2 seconds)?
options: No — useTransition only helps with expensive synchronous renders, not async network requests
Yes — wrapping the fetch in startTransition makes it non-blocking
Yes — React will cancel the fetch if a higher-priority update arrives
Yes — it automatically shows a loading spinner during the fetch
questions.answer: No — useTransition only helps with expensive synchronous renders, not async network requests
questions.explanation: Network requests are already asynchronous — they don't block React's render loop. useTransition solves expensive synchronous work in the render phase: filtering huge arrays, sorting large datasets, building complex derived structures. For slow API responses, use loading state (useState) or TanStack Query's isLoading — not useTransition.
